title: Strong verbs by vowel family
title_target: Jag har inte sprungit sedan skolan
goal: Stop learning strong verbs one by one: sort them into vowel families, and a single pattern will give you dozens of past forms.
bekal: recognize the five big families of strong verbs (*skriva – skrev – skrivit*, *dricka – drack – druckit*…)
form the past and the supine of about forty common strong verbs
talk about your weekend with *flög*, *bjöd*, *sprang*, *satt* and *njöt*
wave: Go back to Unit 1: retell Dian's chaotic first morning aloud in the past, then replace every verb you can with a strong one — *sprang* instead of *gick fort*, *steg på* instead of *tog*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Måndagslunch
dialogs.intro: Dian's second week at the company. On Monday she has lunch with her colleagues Mattias and Leila in the canteen at Lindholmen, and the conversation turns to the weekend.

notes: **Vad hittade du på?** — *hitta på* (**hit-tah POH**) means "to come up with, to get up to": *Vad ska vi hitta på ikväll?* (What shall we do tonight?). Like every particle verb, the stress is on the particle. Without *på*, *hitta* just means "to find".

**Satt** — the past of *sitta*. It belongs to the *i – a – u* family: *sitta – satt – suttit*, just like *dricka – drack – druckit* a few lines further down. Once you know one member, you know them all.

**En mil** (**meel**) is a Swedish mile: **ten kilometers**, not an English mile. Swedes use it constantly for distances and fuel consumption: *bilen drar en halv liter milen* (the car uses half a liter per ten km).

**Bjöd min syster på middag** — *bjuda någon på något* means "to treat someone to something": the person who *bjuder* pays. *Jag bjuder!* = "It's on me!". The past *bjöd* and *flög* both show the *ö* that marks family 3.

**Hon fyllde trettio** — *fylla år* (literally "fill years") means "to have a birthday", and *fylla trettio* is "to turn thirty". *Hon väntar barn*, literally "she is waiting for a child", is the everyday way to say "she's expecting".

**Hållit ett tal** — Swedes *hold* a speech: *hålla tal*. *Hålla* is one of the odd ones out (*hålla – höll – hållit*). You'll need it again in Svenska 104, where Dian gives a wedding speech of her own.

grammars.title: Strong verbs: the vowel tells the story
body: Weak verbs build the past with an ending: *packa → packade*, *läsa → läste*. Strong verbs add **no ending in the past** — they change the **vowel** instead, the way English does with *sing – sang – sung*. The supine then ends in **-it**.
The good news is that most strong verbs belong to a handful of **vowel families**. Learn the family pattern, and every new verb that belongs to it falls into place. Here are the two biggest.
after: The *i – a – u* family is the one English speakers find easiest: *drink – drank – drunk*, *sink – sank – sunk*, *swim – swam – swum* work exactly the same way.
The present tense of strong verbs is perfectly regular: *skriver*, *dricker*, *springer*. Only the past and the supine need to be learned.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Söndagsmiddag i Askim
dialogs.intro: Oskar is living at home in Göteborg this year while he writes his thesis, and his parents have invited Dian to Sunday dinner at their house in Askim, south of the city. She was their guest once before, two years ago. Oskar's mother opens the door.

lines.text: Välkommen, Dian! Det var länge sedan vi sågs.

lines.text: Då lyfter vi glasen. Skål, och välkommen till Göteborg!

notes: **Det var länge sedan vi sågs** — the standard way to say "long time no see". *Sågs* is the past of the reciprocal verb *ses* (see each other) from Svenska 102: *vi ses – vi sågs – vi har setts*.
**Har stått i köket hela dagen** — *stå – stod – stått*. "Standing in the kitchen all day" is the Swedish image for cooking a big meal, said with a mix of pride and complaint.

**For ner till Feskekôrka** — *fara – for – farit* (family *a – o – a*) means "to go, to travel". In Stockholm people mostly say *åka*, but *fara* is very much alive in western and southern Sweden. Don't confuse *for* (**foor**, went) with *för* (**för**, for).

**Feskekôrka** (**FES-keh-shör-kah**) is Göteborg's famous fish market hall from 1874, built to look like a Gothic church. The name is pure dialect: *fesk* for *fisk*, *kôrka* for *kyrka*. Göteborgska has many such words — Unit 16 of Svenska 104 visits the dialects properly.
**Bära in – bar in** — *bära – bar – burit* (family *ä – a – u*). Notice that the particle stays, and still carries the stress, in every tense: *bär IN*, *bar IN*, *har burit IN*.

**Njutit av varje minut** — *njuta av* (**NYÜ-tah ahv**) means "to enjoy", always with *av*: *njuta av solen*, *njuta av maten*. Forms: *njuta – njöt – njutit*. Swedes use it for deep, quiet pleasure, and *Njut!* (Enjoy!) is what a waiter might say as he puts down your plate.

grammars.title: Three more families
body: Family 3 is the biggest. Its infinitive has **y**, **ju** or **u**, and the past always has **ö**. In the supine, *y* becomes *u*, while *ju* usually stays *ju*. Families 4 and 5 are small but full of everyday verbs.
after: *Ta* and *dra* are short forms of the old *taga* and *draga*. The supine keeps the old *g*: *tagit*, *dragit* — which is why they look odd next to their infinitives.
*Slå* has an *å* in the infinitive but behaves exactly like *fara*: *slog*, *slagit*.
Strong verbs also form past participles from the supine stem: *skriven*, *bruten*, *stulen* (*en stulen cykel*). Unit 9 shows how they agree like adjectives.

blocks.text: About fifteen very common verbs follow no family at all. Unfortunately they are among the most frequent words in the language, so there is no way around them — but you already know most of them from Svenska 101 and 102.

blocks.title: How to make them stick
items: Always learn **three forms aloud as one chunk**, with a rhythm: *dricka – drack – druckit*. Your ear will remember the melody before your brain remembers the rule.
When you meet a new strong verb, ask: **which family?** Write it into your own family table instead of a random list.
Practice with a mini-story: *I lördags **sprang** jag, **drack** kaffe, **satt** i solen och **njöt**. Jag har aldrig **njutit** så mycket.*
Write *sa*, but recognize *sade* — it is the written form, and it is pronounced **sah** too.

rows: What did you get up to?

blocks.text: On Monday mornings at a Swedish workplace, *Hur var helgen?* is the ritual question, and a short, honest answer is perfect: *Lugn. Jag sov länge och tog en promenad.* Nobody expects an exciting weekend — in fact, *jag tog det lugnt* is a perfectly respectable thing to have done.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 1
items: Put five strong verbs into the pluperfect: *hade druckit*, *hade skrivit*, *hade flugit*, *hade burit*, *hade sprungit*.
Use each one in a *när*-sentence: *När vi kom fram hade Mattias redan **druckit** upp kaffet.*
Then decide: preteritum or perfekt? *Jag **flög** till Stockholm i fredags* — but *Jag **har** aldrig **flugit** till Kiruna*.
